title: Justice, nearest to taqwa
hook: a thumb near the scale, and the verse that puts fairness next to mindfulness of Allah

segments.voice: Yesterday, rifq, and your line: gentle in all things. Was there one thing you did more gently than usual? Today, a virtue that sounds hard-edged, and the surprising company the Qur'an keeps it in. Day one thousand three hundred twelve.

Grapes go on one side of a market scale, a weight on the other, and a thumb hovers just above the pan. Nobody is watching the thumb. That's the whole drama of fairness: much of it happens where no one is checking. Surah al-Ma'idah gives justice an unexpected neighbor. Not courage. Not law. In Pickthall's translation: "Deal justly, that is nearer to your duty." Today: why fairness sits so close to taqwa, and what that has to do with the thumb.
screen: `A THUMB ABOVE THE PAN.` → `NOBODY IS CHECKING.` → `DEAL JUSTLY, THAT IS NEARER.`

segments.voice: Start with the word Pickthall renders as duty. In the Arabic of the verse it's taqwa: mindfulness of Allah, guarding yourself, keeping watch over what you do. English struggles to hold it in one word, so translators choose different ones. Now look at what the verse says comes nearest to it. Not a long night of prayer. Not a fast. Dealing justly. The word for justice here is 'adl, and its picture is a balance: two sides level, nothing tipped. So the verse makes a quiet claim. Taqwa isn't only something that happens on a prayer mat. It shows up at the counter, in the way a bill gets split, in the way a fight gets retold. Second, the sky and the scale. Surah al-Rahman, in paraphrase: He raised the heaven and set up the balance, so do not cheat the balance; keep the weight fair and don't make the measure short. The sky and the grocer's weight, in the same breath. Third, the home. In Sahih Muslim, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, speaks of people who will be on pulpits of light near Allah. Who are they? In paraphrase: those who are just in their judgments, with their families, and in whatever they're put in charge of. Families. Not only courtrooms. The parent dividing the last slice. The older sister picking teams. The manager handing out the good shifts. And fourth, the same verse in al-Ma'idah won't let dislike off the hook: hatred of a people, it says, must not push anyone away from justice. That's been a day of its own on this path. Today's focus is smaller and closer: fairness as a way of being mindful of Allah, practiced right where the thumb is.
screen: `TAQWA: PICKTHALL SAYS DUTY.` · `'ADL: A BALANCE HELD LEVEL.` · `THE SKY AND THE SCALE TOGETHER.` · `PULPITS OF LIGHT: JUST AT HOME.`

segments.voice: The practice: be fair in one small thing. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind something you'll divide or decide today. Time. Chores. Credit for a piece of work. The last of the food. The way you'll tell someone what happened. Look at it like a scale. Where's your thumb? Is one side yours, and quietly a little heavier? Don't fix everything. Just level that one thing, in your mind, and see it sitting even. If you pray, you can hold the line from al-Ma'idah: deal justly, that is nearer to your duty. The bell holds the time.
Justice. 'Adl: a balance held level, at the market, at home and in judgment, and called in surah al-Ma'idah nearer to taqwa. Today's word.
Your line: nearest to taqwa. Today, find one small scale, a split, a turn, a share of the credit, and keep your thumb off it. Tomorrow, keeping ties. Day one thousand three hundred twelve.

howItsDone: Muslims read al-Ma'idah 5:8 as tying justice to taqwa, and the hadith of the just on pulpits of light extends fairness to judgments, families and anything a person is put in charge of.

original.note: Arabic: justice, balance. in 5:8 the command is i'dilu, deal justly.

trapdoor: what you thought: justice is for courts and governments.
what it means: 'adl is a level balance kept everywhere: the market scale, the family table, the job you're put in charge of.
what a scholar hears: 5:8 ranks justice nearest to taqwa, and Muslim 1827 sets the just on pulpits of light for fairness 'with their families.'
